messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Kiet Tran had been twenty-four when a coordinated bombing tore through the downtown transit hub. He remembered the sudden pressure wave, the screech of twisting metal, and the acrid smoke that swallowed the morning light. In the chaos, his instincts fractured. Instead of helping the bleeding or guiding others to safety, he had crouched behind a shattered ticket kiosk, pressing his palms against his ears until his nails drew blood. That paralysis stuck in his throat. He had come to believe that his freezing had violated every value he held about loyalty and courage. What frightened him most was the certainty that he could no longer rely on himself, a conviction that would soon rewrite his days. Over the following months, that conviction steadily fed his alarm system. Because he was certain he had failed his own standards, his nervous system began treating every ordinary sound as a threat. A car backfiring would send his heart into a frantic rhythm, and a customer’s loud laugh in the bank lobby would trigger an angry outburst that left him staring at his hands in shame. He found himself waking at two in the morning, forced out of bed to check the deadbolt, scan the hallway, and listen to the furnace kick on before he could breathe again. Yet, each time he caught himself snapping at a colleague or pacing the apartment, he took it as proof that he was broken, that he was no longer capable of the steady life he had once planned. The more he felt the threat closing in, the more he internalized his own hypervigilance as evidence of his failure. To keep the panic at bay, Kiet buried himself in his work as a bank teller. The teller cage, with its glass partition and rhythmic cash drawer, became his sanctuary. He traced the bank’s emergency exit maps during lunch breaks, routing his steps along the periphery while the floor hummed around him. He volunteered for Saturday shifts, letting the strict protocols of wire transfers drown out any space where his mind might drift. He pushed past the memory of his ex-wife, refusing to discuss the divorce, telling himself he simply needed to focus on rebuilding. When a dropped pen made him jump, he would suppress the rising panic by diving deeper into the ledger, convincing himself that staying busy would lock the thoughts away. But the more he worked to silence the fear and avoid emotional closeness, the more he felt he was betraying his own nature, retreating into rigid control that left him hollow. By his twenty-sixth birthday, the distance Kiet had built had become a chasm. His marriage unraveled from his slow withdrawal, the way he flinched when she tried to hug him, the clipped sentences he used to answer questions about his day. He saw his exhaustion as the only way to keep the world at a safe distance, yet the exhaustion whispered he was unfit for anything requiring vulnerability. He sat in his quiet apartment, wondering how long he could keep counting the days until he collapsed. What finally brought him to the clinic’s waiting room was the morning he dropped deposit slips during a transfer, his hands trembling too violently to pick them up. He realized he could no longer perform the tasks that anchored him. He was hoping to stop feeling like a stranger in his own life, but he was terrified that sitting still long enough to understand why would let the explosion happen all over again.
